content.title: About
content.content: Tilapia is a freshwater fish from the cichlid family, farm‑raised worldwide. Raw tilapia has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a firm yet tender texture. It is commonly used for frying, baking, grilling, and in sauces.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tilapia is one of the fastest‑growing farmed fish – it reaches market size in 6‑8 months.
The species adapts to a wide range of water conditions and can be fed both plant‑based and animal‑based feeds.
Tilapia is low in fat and high in protein, making it popular among athletes and those watching their weight.
Unlike many marine fish, tilapia contains very low levels of mercury.
Farmed tilapia is often raised in closed‑system recirculating aquaculture, allowing precise control of water quality and nutrition.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Tilapia provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein per 100 g, supporting muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Its low saturated‑fat content makes it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tilapia is a good source of vitamin B12, niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which aid energy metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The fish supplies phosphorus, selenium and potassium, important for bones, antioxidant protection and blood‑pressure regulation.

items.title: Low mercury levels
items.content: Compared with large predatory marine fish, tilapia contains virtually no mercury, making frequent consumption safe.

items.title: Water and feed quality
items.content: Poor water quality or contaminated feed can lead to bacterial or chemical residues in the fish.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tilapia.

items.title: Omega‑3 content
items.content: Tilapia provides less omega‑3 fatty acids than fatty marine fish, so it should not be relied on as the primary source of these nutrients.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw tilapia should be kept refrigerated and cooked soon after purchase. It works well for pan‑frying, oven‑baking, grilling, and in soups or sauces. Before cooking, rinse the fillets under cold water and pat dry with paper towels.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store raw tilapia in an airtight container in the refrigerator at 0‑2 °C for up to 2 days. For longer storage, freeze in a tightly sealed bag at –18 °C for up to 3 months. Thaw completely in the refrigerator before use.
